title: Rubrics from the Task, Verdicts from Evidence:Pointwise Rubric Rewards with Tool-Augmented Judges

paper.title: Rubrics from the Task, Verdicts from Evidence: Pointwise Rubric Rewards with Tool-Augmented Judges
paper.abstract:
Abstract Rubric-based reward models (RMs) evaluate responses against explicit criteria. However, existing methods often derive criteria from observed response candidates, introducing response-induced bias that may limit rubric generalizability.
Their judges also struggle with mechanical constraints when relying on reading alone,
and commonly used pairwise judges provide only relative preferences, complicating their direct use for policy optimization.
We propose ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM that derives hard rules and graded principles by reasoning about the instruction alone and evaluates responses independently through tool-augmented judging. Both components are trained through label-blind distillation, in which preference labels only filter a teacher’s outputs, yielding ReVeR-Traces, a large-scale dataset of rubric-reasoning and judging trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that ReVeR outperforms pairwise rubric RMs in average preference accuracy, most clearly on instruction following, as well as in test-time scaling and downstream policy optimization. We further find that generator RL improves preference accuracy while reducing rubric fidelity, and that higher preference accuracy does not necessarily translate into better downstream policies. These findings highlight that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties, shedding light on future RM research. sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Rubric-based reward models (RMs) are attracting growing attention in LLM post-training for non-verifiable tasks that lack a single correct answer. On such tasks, traditional RMs that assign holistic scalar scores ( Christiano et al., 2017 , Ouyang et al., 2022 , Wang et al., 2024a , Liu et al., 2026c ) can be unreliable ( Hashemi et al., 2024 , Lee et al., 2025 ) . Rubric-based RMs instead evaluate LLM responses against a set of explicit criteria before producing an overall evaluation ( Gunjal et al., 2025 , Viswanathan et al., 2025 , Liu et al., 2026b ) . Typical rubric-based RMs consist of two components: a rubric generator that proposes evaluation criteria for a given instruction, and a judge that evaluates responses against them. To generate discriminative rubrics, existing methods often rely on observed responses. For example, Liu et al. (2026b) , Xu et al. (2026c) first ask a teacher LLM to contrast preferred and rejected responses and propose criteria that distinguish them. A student rubric generator is then fine-tuned on the resulting rubric dataset to predict criteria from the instruction alone. Other approaches analyze multiple candidate responses of varying quality to identify differences or common failure modes, then construct rubrics to distinguish these responses ( Viswanathan et al., 2025 , Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Once such a response-induced rubric is generated, a judge evaluates candidate responses against its criteria. To improve reward-modeling performance, some methods employ pairwise judges that compare two responses side by side and determine which better satisfies the criteria ( Liu et al., 2026b , Xu et al., 2026c ) . Despite their effectiveness, existing rubric-based RMs face limitations in both rubric construction and judging. First, response-induced rubric construction may bias the resulting criteria toward the observed candidates, potentially overlooking task requirements that all candidates satisfy or violate. This bias may limit the generalizability of the resulting rubrics to unseen responses. Moreover, a rubric generator trained on such rubrics may inherit this bias even when it generates criteria from the instruction alone at inference time. Second, complex instructions may involve both mechanical constraints, such as word limits , and subjective quality dimensions, such as vividness of language . However, existing LLM-based judges often evaluate responses by reading them alone. Consequently, even when a rubric correctly identifies mechanical constraints, the judge may still struggle to verify whether a response satisfies them ( Zeng et al., 2024 , Zhang et al., 2024b ) . Furthermore, pairwise judges provide relative preferences rather than independent scores for individual responses, complicating their direct use as rewards in policy optimization. In light of these limitations, we propose ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM. Instead of contrasting responses, our rubric generator derives evaluation criteria by reasoning about the instruction alone, identifying the intended deliverable, explicit and implied requirements, and potential failure modes. These criteria are organized into hard rules for mandatory requirements and principles for graded quality assessment. Moreover, ReVeR’s judge evaluates each response independently under a shared, instruction-specific rubric and uses a sandboxed Python interpreter to verify mechanical constraints while relying on reasoning to assess semantic criteria. The final reward prioritizes hard-rule satisfaction, using graded principle scores to distinguish responses satisfying the same number of hard rules. We train ReVeR through label-blind distillation from a stronger teacher LLM. Specifically, the teacher first generates rubric reasoning from the instruction alone and judges the preferred and rejected responses in separate episodes. Afterwards, the preference labels only select the examples whose scores agree with them and never alter a rubric or a judgment. The teacher thus generates its outputs using only information available to the corresponding students at inference time. This process yields ReVeR-Traces , a dataset containing 30K rubric-reasoning traces and 61K tool-augmented judging trajectories. We further train the rubric generator through a two-stage process, consisting of supervised fine-tuning (ReVeR (SFT)) followed by reinforcement learning (ReVeR (G-RL)). With 4B models, ReVeR achieves higher average preference accuracy and better overall downstream policy performance under DPO and GRPO than 8B pairwise rubric RMs, most clearly on instruction following. Meanwhile, our experiments reveal that these evaluation dimensions do not necessarily align: generator RL improves preference accuracy while reducing rubric fidelity, and under GRPO the most accurate pairwise rubric RM yields a policy that asserts its own compliance and falls below the base policy on IFEval. These findings highlight that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties that should be evaluated separately. Our contributions are: • We present ReVeR, a 4B pointwise rubric RM that derives typed rubrics from the instruction alone and employs a tool-augmented judge. • We introduce ReVeR-Traces, a large and diverse dataset containing rich rubric-reasoning traces and judging trajectories, which is released along with our model checkpoints. • We show that ReVeR achieves higher average preference accuracy than pairwise rubric RMs, leading on every instruction-following benchmark, and achieves stronger average downstream performance under DPO and GRPO. We also reveal that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties, shedding light on future RM research.

sections.heading: Rubric and checklist rewards.
sections.text: Rubrics and checklists decompose evaluation into explicit criteria ( Liu et al., 2023 , Hashemi et al., 2024 , Kim et al., 2025 , Lin et al., 2025 , Arora et al., 2025 , Starace et al., 2025 ) . They serve as reinforcement-learning rewards ( Gunjal et al., 2025 ; RLCF, Viswanathan et al., 2025 ), as supervision for rubric generators and rubric-conditioned judges ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , and as components optimized jointly with the judge, pairwise in Xu et al. (2026c) , and pointwise in Jiang et al. (2026) . Some criteria are written from the instruction, either by a prompted model ( Cook et al., 2024 ) or by a trained reward model that gives each response one overall score ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . Others are induced from observed responses, either from preferred and rejected answers ( Liu et al., 2026b , Xie et al., 2025 , Liu et al., 2026a ) or from the failure modes of sampled candidates ( Viswanathan et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, ReVeR derives its criteria from the instruction by reasoning about the task, distills that reasoning into a small generator, and returns one verdict per criterion for each response.

sections.heading: Reasoning and tool-augmented judges.
sections.text: LLM judges are prompted or trained to evaluate responses ( Zheng et al., 2023 , Li et al., 2024a , Vu et al., 2024 ) , and generative reward models reason before giving a verdict ( Zhang et al., 2024a , Chen et al., 2026 , Whitehouse et al., 2026 ) . Some systems add evidence retrieved by search ( Wei et al., 2024 ) , gathered by an agent ( Zhuge et al., 2024 ) , or produced by executed code. RewardAgent routes instruction constraints to a code-based verifier and combines its output with a preference model ( Peng et al., 2025 ) , and TIR-Judge trains judges with tool-integrated reinforcement learning ( Xu et al., 2026b ) . ReVeR lets the judge decide per criterion whether execution is needed and trains it by distillation alone (Table 1 a).

sections.heading: Open data for training evaluators.
sections.text: Open resources for training rubric generators and judges differ in what they record (Table 1 b). OpenRubrics ( Liu et al., 2026b ) pairs contrastively written rubrics with pairwise judge rationales, and RUBRIC-ARROW with per-criterion labels for single responses. WildChecklists ( Viswanathan et al., 2025 ) holds checklists written from sampled responses, and RubricHub ( Li et al., 2026 ) holds rubrics written from a reference response. Feedback Collection ( Kim et al., 2023 ) and R3 ( Anugraha et al., 2025 ) attach written feedback and distilled reasoning to scored responses. ReVeR-Traces records the reasoning behind each rubric and the tool-augmented trajectory behind each verdict, both generated label-blind.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: We propose ReVeR, which evaluates a response by rubric generation, tool-augmented verdicts, and fine-grained aggregation, as depicted in Fig. 1 .

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Formulation
sections.text: Let x x be an instruction, including any context, and y y a response. A rubric R = { ( c i , t i ) } i = 1 k R=\{(c_{i},t_{i})\}_{i=1}^{k} is a set of natural-language criteria c i c_{i} , each typed as a hard rule or a principle . A generator G θ G_{\theta} writes reasoning z z and a rubric; a judge J ϕ J_{\phi} with a Python interpreter produces a trajectory τ \tau that ends in one verdict per criterion; and an aggregator S S maps the verdict scores q ⁡ ( τ ) = ( s 1 , … , s k ) q(\tau)=(s_{1},\dots,s_{k}) to a reward: ( z , R ) ∼ G θ ( ⋅ ∣ x ) , τ ∼ J ϕ ( ⋅ ∣ x , y , R ) , r ⁡ ( x , y ) = S ⁡ ( q ⁡ ( τ ) , R ) . \begin{gathered}(z,R)\sim G_{\theta}(\,\cdot\mid x),\quad\tau\sim J_{\phi}(\,\cdot\mid x,y,R),\\ r(x,y)=S\bigl(q(\tau);R\bigr).\end{gathered} (1) The conditioning sets in Eq. 1 determine two properties. Prompt-level rubrics : R R depends only on x x , so one rubric is generated per prompt and shared by every response to it, and all candidates are measured against the same criteria. Pointwise verdicts : τ \tau depends only on ( x , y , R ) (x,y,R) , so r ⁡ ( x , y ) r(x,y) is invariant to the other responses under consideration and to the order in which they are presented, which is known to bias LLM judges ( Wang et al., 2024b , Shi et al., 2025 ) . A pairwise judge assigns no value to a single response ( Liusie et al., 2024 , Liu et al., 2024b ) .

sections.heading: 3.2 Task-Derived Rubric Generation
sections.text: The generator conditions on the instruction alone and factorizes as p θ ​ ( z , R ∣ x ) = p θ ​ ( z ∣ x ) ​ p θ ​ ( R ∣ x , z ) p_{\theta}(z,R\mid x)=p_{\theta}(z\mid x)\,p_{\theta}(R\mid x,z) , reasoning about the task before writing criteria. The reasoning z z identifies the deliverable the user wants, the explicit requirements and how binding each is, the expectations a competent reader infers from the task, and the ways a response could fail while appearing relevant. Each criterion is then typed. A hard rule is an explicit, non-negotiable requirement whose violation makes a response unacceptable; a principle is a quality dimension that a response satisfies to a degree. The type fixes how a criterion is scored and prioritized (§ 3.3 ) and is independent of how it is checked, so a hard rule can be decided by reading. The generator is asked to keep a criterion only if it follows from the instruction or the task type, can be met by substantively different high-quality responses, stays useful for unseen responses, captures a condition of success or failure, and is not redundant (Appendix F ). The tests keep the rubric a statement about the task, so it encodes functional requirements that every acceptable response meets, including those that no pair of responses separates. sections.text: The judge scores one response per episode. An episode is a trajectory τ = ( ( u t , a t , o t ) t = 1 m − 1 , u m , v ) , \tau=\bigl((u_{t},a_{t},o_{t})_{t=1}^{m-1},\;u_{m},\;v\bigr), (2) where u t u_{t} is reasoning, a t a_{t} is a Python program ( Gao et al., 2023 , Chen et al., 2022 , Yao et al., 2022 ) , o t = Exec ⁡ ( a t ) o_{t}=\Exec(a_{t}) is its output or error, and v v is the final set of verdicts. A budget B B bounds the number of executed programs, so m ≤ B + 1 m\leq B+1 .

sections.heading: Evidence.
sections.text: Whatever its type, a criterion is mechanical if its truth is a computable function of the response string: word, sentence, or paragraph counts, prefix and case checks, forbidden terms, pattern matches, format validity, and arithmetic. The verdict on a mechanical criterion is meant to rest on an executed output o t o_{t} ; the verdict on a semantic criterion, such as relevance or reasoning quality, rests on the judge’s reasoning over y y . The judge decides which criteria need execution and consolidates their checks into one program per step, and a verdict may cite only an output that was returned.

A target sequence can be reproduced only from information in the student’s input. Rubric reasoning written after reading ( y + , y − ) (y^{+},y^{-}) is a sample from 𝒯 ( ⋅ ∣ x , y + , y − ) \mathcal{T}(\,\cdot\mid x,y^{+},y^{-}) , while the student models p θ ​ ( z , R ∣ x ) p_{\theta}(z,R\mid x) . We therefore sample the teacher under the students’ conditioning sets. Given a preference triple d = ( x , y + , y − ) d=(x,y^{+},y^{-}) , ( z , R ) ∼ 𝒯 ( ⋅ ∣ x ) , τ ± ∼ 𝒯 ( ⋅ ∣ x , y ± , R ) , (z,R)\sim\mathcal{T}(\,\cdot\mid x),\quad\tau^{\pm}\sim\mathcal{T}(\,\cdot\mid x,y^{\pm},R), (4) with the two responses judged in separate episodes under the same rubric. The preference label is used once, after generation, in an acceptance test: A ( d ) = 𝟏 [ valid ( d ) ] ⋅ 𝟏 [ S 𝒯 + > S 𝒯 − ] , A(d)=\mathbf{1}\bigl[\mathrm{valid}(d)\bigr]\cdot\mathbf{1}\bigl[S_{\mathcal{T}}^{+}>S_{\mathcal{T}}^{-}\bigr], (5) where S 𝒯 ± = S 𝒯 ​ ( x , y ± , R ) S_{\mathcal{T}}^{\pm}=S_{\mathcal{T}}(x,y^{\pm};R) and valid ⁡ ( d ) \mathrm{valid}(d) holds when the rubric and both trajectories are well-formed. We call the procedure label-blind because neither the preference label nor the competing response is in context when a rubric or a trajectory is generated. Acceptance is rejection sampling from the teacher’s own distributions. It selects which samples are kept and leaves their content unchanged, so every retained sequence was generated only from information the student has at inference. Each accepted triple yields one generator example ( x , z , R ) (x,z,R) and two judge examples ( x , y ± , R , τ ± ) (x,y^{\pm},R,\tau^{\pm}) . Both students are trained by maximum likelihood on the full target sequences: the generator on ( z , R ) (z,R) given x x , and the judge on its reasoning, programs, and verdicts given ( x , y , R ) (x,y,R) and the preceding steps. The judge conditions on program outputs and does not predict them.

sections.heading: 3.5 ReVeR-Traces
sections.text: ReVeR-Traces applies label-blind distillation to five preference datasets: HelpSteer3 ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , UltraFeedback ( Cui et al., 2024 ) , Skywork-Reward ( Liu et al., 2024a ) , Magpie ( Xu et al., 2024 ) , and IFEval-like instructions from OpenRubrics ( Liu et al., 2026b ) ; the teacher is DeepSeek-V4-Flash ( Xu et al., 2026a ) at high reasoning effort. Of 41,388 preference triples, 30,310 (73.2%) pass the acceptance test, giving 30,310 rubric-reasoning traces and 60,620 judging trajectories, two per retained pair (Fig. 2 ). Each triple is sampled once, and 74.2% of the rejections are reversed preferences, 19.5% ties, and 6.3% invalid outputs (Appendix B ). Rubrics average 4.9 criteria, 56% of them hard rules, and a program is called in 58.9% of the trajectories. Generated label-blind, the teacher’s reasoning records how it reached a judgment in place of a justification for a known outcome ( Turpin et al., 2023 ) . We release both subsets with ReVeR (SFT), ReVeR (G-RL), and the judging harness.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: This section asks three questions: how accurately ReVeR ranks a preferred response above a rejected one (§ 4.1 ), how well its reward serves best-of- N N selection and policy training (§ 4.2 ), and how closely its rubrics agree with expert rubrics (§ 4.3 ). We compare ReVeR with the reasoning reward models RM-R1 ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , RRM ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , and JudgeLRM ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , the rubric-based reward models Rubric-RM, Rubric-ARM, CE-RM, and PaTaRM ( Jian et al., 2026 ) , and the tool-augmented TIR-Judge. Baseline numbers are taken from the original papers where reported and computed with the released models otherwise. Appendices B and F give the training and evaluation details and both prompts.

sections.heading: What training on ReVeR-Traces contributes.
sections.text: Under the same judging protocol, the untrained Qwen3.5-4B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) , as both generator and judge, averages 57.0. ReVeR (SFT) reaches 68.1, 11.1 points higher and 3.6 below its teacher.

sections.heading: Comparison with other reward models.
sections.text: ReVeR has the two highest averages among single-judgment reward models, 69.1 with ReVeR (G-RL) and 68.1 with ReVeR (SFT), ahead of Rubric-ARM-8B (66.3) and of the 32B reasoning models RRM (65.8) and RM-R1 (65.6). It leads on every instruction-following column and on RubricBench Chat: 83.3 on IFEval, 75.9 on IFBench, 55.0 on the instruction-following subset of RewardBench 2, where the best other model reaches 41.9, and 52.7 and 62.1 on RubricBench, against 49.6 and 53.7. The 32B reasoning models rank first on RewardBench, RM-Bench, and JudgeBench, with 95.3 on RewardBench Chat against 85.4 for the better ReVeR configuration, and Rubric-ARM ranks first on the Focus subset of RewardBench 2.

sections.heading: Generator RL and repeated judgments.
sections.text: With the judge shared, ReVeR (G-RL) averages 1.0 point above ReVeR (SFT). With five judgments per response, the two averages rise to 73.5 and 73.8, above the single judgment of the teacher (71.7).

sections.heading: Best-of- N N selection and test-time scaling.
sections.text: For each prompt of IFEval ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) and MulDimIF ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , we sample sixteen candidates from a frozen Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , score each once under one rubric, and select the best of N N ( Snell et al., 2024 ) . IFEval is the mean of its four accuracies. ReVeR selects better responses than every baseline at every N N (Fig. 3 ). At N = 16 N=16 both configurations reach 85.1 on IFEval and 60.3 on MulDimIF, 3.7 and 5.1 points above the strongest baseline and 9.8 and 11.1 points above a single sample. ReVeR obtains 67% and 55% of that gain, and the strongest baseline 41% and 30%. With four candidates, both configurations already exceed every baseline at sixteen. sections.heading: Policy training.
sections.text: We train policies from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct under DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) and under GRPO, each with one of four rewards: ReVeR (SFT), ReVeR (G-RL), and the pairwise Rubric-RM-8B and Rubric-ARM-8B. For DPO, each reward picks the best and the worst of eight sampled responses as a preference pair; for GRPO, the ReVeR score of each rollout is its reward (Appendix B ). We evaluate every policy on IFEval, IFBench ( Pyatkin et al., 2026 ) , MulDimIF, and Arena-Hard v1 ( Li et al., 2024b ) with and without style control.

sections.heading: Preference optimization.
sections.text: Under DPO, the best value in every column of Table 3 belongs to a policy trained with ReVeR. The average rises from 53.9 for the base policy to 57.9 with ReVeR (SFT) and 57.4 with ReVeR (G-RL), against 55.1 with Rubric-RM-8B and 55.5 with Rubric-ARM-8B. The margin of ReVeR (SFT) over Rubric-ARM-8B is widest where compliance is checked strictly: 77.1 against 73.9 on prompt-level strict IFEval accuracy, and 58.7 against 54.4 on MulDimIF.

sections.heading: Online RL.
sections.text: Under GRPO, ReVeR again reaches the two highest averages, 57.4 with ReVeR (G-RL) and 56.6 with ReVeR (SFT), against 55.1 with Rubric-RM-8B and 51.8 with Rubric-ARM-8B. It gives the best value in every instruction-following column. ReVeR (G-RL) further improves Arena-Hard performance, raising scores from 52.5 with ReVeR (SFT) to 54.6 and 56.0 under the style-controlled and vanilla settings, respectively. We also find that, under GRPO with the Rubric-ARM-8B reward, preference and compliance come apart. Its policy reaches 62.0 on Arena-Hard without style control, 9.1 points above the base policy, and the gain shrinks to 2.5 points once style is controlled. At the same time, its IFEval average falls to 73.8 and its MulDimIF accuracy to 39.3, below the base policy’s 77.0 and 51.7, with prompt-level strict IFEval accuracy at 63.4 against 72.1. The policy has learned to certify its own compliance, a pattern consistent with reward hacking ( Amodei et al., 2016 , Skalse et al., 2022 , Raina et al., 2024 ) . Of its 541 IFEval responses, 133 end with a summary or self-assessment and 56 of these explicitly claim compliance, against 10 and 1 for the base policy, 17 and 1 with Rubric-RM-8B, and at most 23 and 2 for the policies trained with ReVeR (Appendix C ). A judge without tools can check such a claim only by reading the response; ReVeR settles a word limit from the count a program returns (§ 3.3 ), which a claim of compliance cannot alter. sections.heading: What distillation learns.
sections.text: ReVeR (SFT) is closest to the expert rubrics on all six measures (Table 4 a). Its F1 reaches 32.1 on chat and 46.3 on instruction following, against 23.6 and 34.9 for Rubric-ARM-8B, the closer of the two baselines. Most of the gain is in precision, 13.3 and 16.4 points above Rubric-ARM-8B, while recall is 2.2 and 3.4 points above Rubric-RM-8B, which has the higher recall of the two. Both baselines learn their rubrics from contrasts between responses; ReVeR’s distilled generator, which the pairs reach only through the acceptance test, comes closer than either to the criteria that experts write.

sections.heading: What generator RL changes.
sections.text: Once the pairs act as a reward, agreement falls on every measure, but ReVeR (G-RL) remains above both baselines in precision and F1. Its rubrics shift from hard rules to principles (Table 4 b), with the share of hard rules falling from 48.2% to 37.8% on chat and from 66.1% to 52.5% on instruction following. Precision falls because principles, which match expert criteria less often than hard rules, become more numerous and match less often than before, whereas hard rules match almost as often as before. The fall in recall comes almost entirely from hard rules (Appendix D ). On instruction following, many of the expert criteria that drop out are explicit, binary requirements such as writing entirely in Spanish, and the principles that enter name generic qualities such as accuracy.

sections.heading: Fidelity and utility.
sections.text: Lower agreement with experts leaves preference accuracy almost unchanged. On the same RubricBench prompts, ReVeR (G-RL) has a preference accuracy of 52.3 on chat and 62.1 on instruction following, against 52.7 and 61.0 for ReVeR (SFT) (Table 2 ). Eq. 6 gives a rubric no reward when the two responses tie, and graded principles separate responses that binary hard rules leave tied. RL therefore shifts rubrics towards principles, and ties fall from 3.5% to 0.9% of pairs on chat and from 4.1% to 1.4% on instruction following. Pairs decided by principles are judged less accurately than pairs decided by hard rules, which offsets the gain from fewer ties (Appendix D ). Generator RL optimizes discrimination between responses, and fidelity is a separate property that preference benchmarks do not measure.

sections.heading: 4.4 Case Study
sections.text: Instruction. … Which college would you recommend? … be sure the letter p appears at least 15 times in your response. Responses. Both ask for the user’s preferences and name no college. A contains 16 p’s and B contains 13. Expert label: A. Shared hard rule. ReVeR: “The response contains at least 15 occurrences of the lowercase letter ‘p’.” Rubric-ARM: “The response must contain at least 15 instances of the letter p.” ReVeR judge , one program per response: response.count(’p’) returns 16 for A and 13 for B. Scores 3.10 and 2.00; it prefers A in 6 of 6 runs. Rubric-ARM judge , reading both responses. Order (A, B): “only Response B satisfies the crucial letter-p count gatekeeper.” Order (B, A): both “fail … the letter-p count gatekeeper” and B “at least reaches closer to 15 p’s.” It prefers B in both orders of 3 of 3 repeats. Figure 4 : Case study on the tool-augmented judge. Given the same criterion, ReVeR’s judge succeeds by running a program and Rubric-ARM’s judge fails. As an illustration, on the RubricBench prompt of Fig. 4 , ReVeR and Rubric-ARM write the same hard rule and prefer opposite responses. ReVeR’s judge counts with a program and prefers Response A, which satisfies the rule, in all six runs; Rubric-ARM’s pairwise judge reads and prefers Response B in both presentation orders of all three repeats (Appendix E ).

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We present ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM, and ReVeR-Traces, a collection of reasoning traces for rubric generation and tool-augmented judgment trajectories. Its generator derives criteria by reasoning about the task, its judge reaches each verdict from the response and from evidence it executes, and both are trained by label-blind distillation. With 4B models, ReVeR has the highest average preference accuracy on reward-model benchmarks among single-judgment reward models, and it improves on pairwise rubric rewards in agreement with expert rubrics, best-of- N N selection, and policy optimization. We also find that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties of a reward and have to be measured separately.

sections.text: Responses that the benchmark prefers concentrate at the high end, with 47% (SFT) and 33% (G-RL) of their scores at 80 or above. sections.text: The two distributions overlap: 28% and 19% of the scores given to rejected responses are 80 or above. On the 41–42% of pairs whose responses tie on hard rules, the principle average favours the preferred response in 58–59%. This supports the aggregation of Eq. 3 , which ranks responses by hard rules first and uses the principle average to break ties. On RubricBench, pairs decided by hard rules are also judged more accurately than pairs decided by principles (Appendix D ).

sections.text: G-RL rubrics contain more principles than SFT rubrics, 2.7 against 1.9 per response, and their principles receive lower scores, with a mean of 48.5 against 55.5.

sections.heading: Judging protocol.
sections.text: A response is scored with one rubric per prompt and one judging episode with B = 3 B=3 . A program runs with a timeout of three seconds. A call that fails can be repaired with a remaining call, which can also run a follow-up check. Once the budget is spent, the judge is instructed to complete its verdicts from the response, to name the missing result in the explanations it affects, and never to claim a verification; a required property without sufficient evidence counts as not satisfied (Appendix F ). A trajectory whose verdicts fail validation, which requires exactly one in-range score per criterion, is resampled, and a response left without valid verdicts receives no score. A response without a valid judgment counts as an error on preference benchmarks, is skipped in selection, and receives no reward in policy training. The benchmark subsets of Table 2 follow the evaluations of Rubric-RM and Rubric-ARM ( Liu et al., 2026b , Xu et al., 2026c ) .

sections.heading: ReVeR-Traces records.
sections.text: A rubric record pairs an instruction with the teacher’s reasoning and typed rubric; a judging record adds one response, the complete trajectory with programs and their outputs, and the per-criterion explanations and scores. The median trace and trajectory run to 2.0K and 3.1K generated tokens (Fig. 2 ). A program fails, by an exception or a timeout, in 17.2% of the trajectories, which is 29.1% of the program calls. With B = 1 B=1 the teacher cannot repair it, so these verdicts follow the rule of the judging protocol, and the triple is retained only if its scores still reproduce the preference. The IFEval-like instructions are part of OpenRubrics ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , make up 1,570 of the 30,310 retained triples, and share no prompt with the IFEval and IFBench prompts used in evaluation.

sections.heading: Acceptance test.
sections.text: The acceptance test of Eq. 5 is applied once to each triple. The teacher writes one rubric and two trajectories, and nothing is resampled when the scores disagree with the label. Of the 11,078 rejected triples, 74.2% reverse the preference, 19.5% tie, and 6.3% are invalid, so the test mostly removes teacher judgments that contradict the human label. Ties, in which the rubric and its verdicts do not separate the two responses, are 5.2% of all triples. The test retains 67.9% of the triples of HelpSteer3, 83.1% of UltraFeedback, 75.0% of Skywork-Reward, 71.2% of Magpie, and 77.2% of the IFEval-like instructions.

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare with three groups of systems. Reasoning reward models reason before giving a verdict: RM-R1, RRM, and JudgeLRM. Rubric-based reward models condition the verdict on generated criteria: Rubric-RM, Rubric-ARM, CE-RM, and PaTaRM. Tool-augmented judges are represented by TIR-Judge. Two references show what training contributes: the untrained Qwen3.5-4B under the same judging protocol, and the teacher, DeepSeek-V4-Flash.

sections.heading: E.1 A Case Decided by the Judge
sections.text: This is the case of § 4.4 . The two rubrics contain the same hard rule on the letter p, and the two judges apply it differently.

sections.heading: Instruction.
sections.text: I’m interested in a college with open enrollment and a regional accreditation. Which college would you recommend? Don’t include the keywords “DuPage” and “Dade” in your response. Let’s make it a constrained writing problem: be sure the letter p appears at least 15 times in your response.

sections.heading: Expert label.
sections.text: Response A is better.

sections.heading: Response A.
sections.text: Choosing the perfect college is a very personal decision, and it’s great you’re prioritizing open enrollment and regional accreditation. To give you a helpful recommendation, I need a little more information about your preferences. For example, what are your academic interests? Are you looking for a primarily online program or a more traditional campus experience? Tell me more about what’s important to you in a college, and I can provide a more specific suggestion. Remember, finding the right fit is crucial for a positive and successful educational experience.

sections.heading: Response B.
sections.text: Choosing a college is a big decision! It’s great that you’re prioritizing open enrollment and regional accreditation, as those are important factors for a quality education. To give you the best recommendation, I need a little more information about your preferences. For example: * **What part of the country are you interested in?** * **Are you looking for a two-year or four-year program?** * **What are your academic interests?** Once I have a better understanding of what you’re looking for, I can provide a more personalized suggestion. Remember, finding the right college is a process, so don’t be afraid to explore your options and ask lots of questions! Let me know if you have any other details you’d like to share. I’m here to help!

sections.heading: Expert rubric.
sections.text: • Does the response explicitly state that the recommended college has an “open enrollment” policy? • Does the response explicitly state that the recommended college has “regional accreditation”? • Does the response avoid including the words “DuPage” and “Dade”? • Does the response contain the letter ’p’ at least 15 times? • Does the response provide a specific, named college or university as a recommendation? • Is the response presented as a continuous paragraph without bullet points or lists?

sections.heading: Rubric of ReVeR (SFT).
sections.text: 1. The response recommends a specific named college that meets both the open enrollment and regional accreditation criteria. [Hard Rule] 2. However, existing methods often derive criteria from observed response candidates, introducing response-induced bias that may limit rubric generalizability. Their judges also struggle with mechanical constraints when relying on reading alone, and commonly used pairwise judges provide only relative preferences, complicating their direct use for policy optimization. We propose ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM that derives hard rules and graded principles by reasoning about the instruction alone and evaluates responses independently through tool-augmented judging. Both components are trained through label-blind distillation, in which preference labels only filter a teacher’s outputs, yielding ReVeR-Traces, a large-scale dataset of rubric-reasoning and judging trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that ReVeR outperforms pairwise rubric RMs in average preference accuracy, most clearly on instruction following, as well as in test-time scaling and downstream policy optimization. We further find that generator RL improves preference accuracy while reducing rubric fidelity, and that higher preference accuracy does not necessarily translate into better downstream policies. These findings highlight that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties, shedding light on future RM research. Keywords: Rubric Reward Model, Agent, RLHF = Date : October 13, 2026 = Model Weights & Checkpoints : https://huggingface.co/OpenRubrics/ReVeR = Datasets : https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenRubrics/ReVeR-Traces-Rubric ; = Datasets : https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenRubrics/ReVeR-Traces-Judge = Contact : tliu43@utk.edu ; hwang28@albany.edu 1 Introduction Rubric-based reward models (RMs) are attracting growing attention in LLM post-training for non-verifiable tasks that lack a single correct answer. On such tasks, traditional RMs that assign holistic scalar scores ( Christiano et al., 2017 , Ouyang et al., 2022 , Wang et al., 2024a , Liu et al., 2026c ) can be unreliable ( Hashemi et al., 2024 , Lee et al., 2025 ) . Rubric-based RMs instead evaluate LLM responses against a set of explicit criteria before producing an overall evaluation ( Gunjal et al., 2025 , Viswanathan et al., 2025 , Liu et al., 2026b ) . Typical rubric-based RMs consist of two components: a rubric generator that proposes evaluation criteria for a given instruction, and a judge that evaluates responses against them. To generate discriminative rubrics, existing methods often rely on observed responses. For example, Liu et al. (2026b) , Xu et al. (2026c) first ask a teacher LLM to contrast preferred and rejected responses and propose criteria that distinguish them. A student rubric generator is then fine-tuned on the resulting rubric dataset to predict criteria from the instruction alone. Other approaches analyze multiple candidate responses of varying quality to identify differences or common failure modes, then construct rubrics to distinguish these responses ( Viswanathan et al., 2025 , Zhang et al., 2025a ) . Once such a response-induced rubric is generated, a judge evaluates candidate responses against its criteria. To improve reward-modeling performance, some methods employ pairwise judges that compare two responses side by side and determine which better satisfies the criteria ( Liu et al., 2026b , Xu et al., 2026c ) . Despite their effectiveness, existing rubric-based RMs face limitations in both rubric construction and judging. First, response-induced rubric construction may bias the resulting criteria toward the observed candidates, potentially overlooking task requirements that all candidates satisfy or violate. This bias may limit the generalizability of the resulting rubrics to unseen responses. Moreover, a rubric generator trained on such rubrics may inherit this bias even when it generates criteria from the instruction alone at inference time. Second, complex instructions may involve both mechanical constraints, such as word limits , and subjective quality dimensions, such as vividness of language . However, existing LLM-based judges often evaluate responses by reading them alone. Consequently, even when a rubric correctly identifies mechanical constraints, the judge may still struggle to verify whether a response satisfies them ( Zeng et al., 2024 , Zhang et al., 2024b ) . Furthermore, pairwise judges provide relative preferences rather than independent scores for individual responses, complicating their direct use as rewards in policy optimization. In light of these limitations, we propose ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM. Instead of contrasting responses, our rubric generator derives evaluation criteria by reasoning about the instruction alone, identifying the intended deliverable, explicit and implied requirements, and potential failure modes. These criteria are organized into hard rules for mandatory requirements and principles for graded quality assessment. Moreover, ReVeR’s judge evaluates each response independently under a shared, instruction-specific rubric and uses a sandboxed Python interpreter to verify mechanical constraints while relying on reasoning to assess semantic criteria. The final reward prioritizes hard-rule satisfaction, using graded principle scores to distinguish responses satisfying the same number of hard rules. We train ReVeR through label-blind distillation from a stronger teacher LLM. Specifically, the teacher first generates rubric reasoning from the instruction alone and judges the preferred and rejected responses in separate episodes. Afterwards, the preference labels only select the examples whose scores agree with them and never alter a rubric or a judgment. The teacher thus generates its outputs using only information available to the corresponding students at inference time. This process yields ReVeR-Traces , a dataset containing 30K rubric-reasoning traces and 61K tool-augmented judging trajectories. We further train the rubric generator through a two-stage process, consisting of supervised fine-tuning (ReVeR (SFT)) followed by reinforcement learning (ReVeR (G-RL)). With 4B models, ReVeR achieves higher average preference accuracy and better overall downstream policy performance under DPO and GRPO than 8B pairwise rubric RMs, most clearly on instruction following. Meanwhile, our experiments reveal that these evaluation dimensions do not necessarily align: generator RL improves preference accuracy while reducing rubric fidelity, and under GRPO the most accurate pairwise rubric RM yields a policy that asserts its own compliance and falls below the base policy on IFEval. These findings highlight that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties that should be evaluated separately. Our contributions are: • We present ReVeR, a 4B pointwise rubric RM that derives typed rubrics from the instruction alone and employs a tool-augmented judge. • We introduce ReVeR-Traces, a large and diverse dataset containing rich rubric-reasoning traces and judging trajectories, which is released along with our model checkpoints. • We show that ReVeR achieves higher average preference accuracy than pairwise rubric RMs, leading on every instruction-following benchmark, and achieves stronger average downstream performance under DPO and GRPO. Rubrics and checklists decompose evaluation into explicit criteria ( Liu et al., 2023 , Hashemi et al., 2024 , Kim et al., 2025 , Lin et al., 2025 , Arora et al., 2025 , Starace et al., 2025 ) . They serve as reinforcement-learning rewards ( Gunjal et al., 2025 ; RLCF, Viswanathan et al., 2025 ), as supervision for rubric generators and rubric-conditioned judges ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , and as components optimized jointly with the judge, pairwise in Xu et al. (2026c) , and pointwise in Jiang et al. (2026) . Some criteria are written from the instruction, either by a prompted model ( Cook et al., 2024 ) or by a trained reward model that gives each response one overall score ( Hu et al., 2026 ) . Others are induced from observed responses, either from preferred and rejected answers ( Liu et al., 2026b , Xie et al., 2025 , Liu et al., 2026a ) or from the failure modes of sampled candidates ( Viswanathan et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, ReVeR derives its criteria from the instruction by reasoning about the task, distills that reasoning into a small generator, and returns one verdict per criterion for each response. Reasoning and tool-augmented judges. LLM judges are prompted or trained to evaluate responses ( Zheng et al., 2023 , Li et al., 2024a , Vu et al., 2024 ) , and generative reward models reason before giving a verdict ( Zhang et al., 2024a , Chen et al., 2026 , Whitehouse et al., 2026 ) . Some systems add evidence retrieved by search ( Wei et al., 2024 ) , gathered by an agent ( Zhuge et al., 2024 ) , or produced by executed code. ReVeR (SFT) is closest to the expert rubrics on all six measures (Table 4 a). Its F1 reaches 32.1 on chat and 46.3 on instruction following, against 23.6 and 34.9 for Rubric-ARM-8B, the closer of the two baselines. Most of the gain is in precision, 13.3 and 16.4 points above Rubric-ARM-8B, while recall is 2.2 and 3.4 points above Rubric-RM-8B, which has the higher recall of the two. Both baselines learn their rubrics from contrasts between responses; ReVeR’s distilled generator, which the pairs reach only through the acceptance test, comes closer than either to the criteria that experts write. What generator RL changes. Once the pairs act as a reward, agreement falls on every measure, but ReVeR (G-RL) remains above both baselines in precision and F1. Its rubrics shift from hard rules to principles (Table 4 b), with the share of hard rules falling from 48.2% to 37.8% on chat and from 66.1% to 52.5% on instruction following. Precision falls because principles, which match expert criteria less often than hard rules, become more numerous and match less often than before, whereas hard rules match almost as often as before. The fall in recall comes almost entirely from hard rules (Appendix D ). On instruction following, many of the expert criteria that drop out are explicit, binary requirements such as writing entirely in Spanish, and the principles that enter name generic qualities such as accuracy. Fidelity and utility. Lower agreement with experts leaves preference accuracy almost unchanged. On the same RubricBench prompts, ReVeR (G-RL) has a preference accuracy of 52.3 on chat and 62.1 on instruction following, against 52.7 and 61.0 for ReVeR (SFT) (Table 2 ). Eq. 6 gives a rubric no reward when the two responses tie, and graded principles separate responses that binary hard rules leave tied. RL therefore shifts rubrics towards principles, and ties fall from 3.5% to 0.9% of pairs on chat and from 4.1% to 1.4% on instruction following. Pairs decided by principles are judged less accurately than pairs decided by hard rules, which offsets the gain from fewer ties (Appendix D ). Generator RL optimizes discrimination between responses, and fidelity is a separate property that preference benchmarks do not measure. 4.4 Case Study Instruction. … Which college would you recommend? … be sure the letter p appears at least 15 times in your response. ReVeR’s judge counts with a program and prefers Response A, which satisfies the rule, in all six runs; Rubric-ARM’s pairwise judge reads and prefers Response B in both presentation orders of all three repeats (Appendix E ). 5 Conclusion We present ReVeR, a pointwise rubric RM, and ReVeR-Traces, a collection of reasoning traces for rubric generation and tool-augmented judgment trajectories. Its generator derives criteria by reasoning about the task, its judge reaches each verdict from the response and from evidence it executes, and both are trained by label-blind distillation. With 4B models, ReVeR has the highest average preference accuracy on reward-model benchmarks among single-judgment reward models, and it improves on pairwise rubric rewards in agreement with expert rubrics, best-of- N N selection, and policy optimization. We also find that rubric fidelity, preference accuracy, and downstream utility are distinct properties of a reward and have to be measured separately.
